title: Tenali Raman Tale 141

full_text:
An elderly, impoverished court copyist named Shastriji dropped his worn, ancient iron writing stylus (*ghantam*) into the deep palace water reservoir.
The stylus was thirty years old, its wooden grip worn smooth by decades of copying sacred scriptures and imperial decrees.
Shastriji sat on the stone steps of the reservoir, weeping bitterly, unable to earn his daily bread without his writing tool.

Tenali Raman saw the old scholar weeping and dove into the clear, deep water.
Tenali surfaced holding a magnificent stylus crafted of solid, gleaming twenty-four-karat gold, encrusted with rubies!
'Is this thy writing stylus, Shastriji?' asked Tenali.

Old Shastriji looked at the dazzling golden tool, blinked through his tears, and shook his head with simple honesty:
'No, noble Tenali. That golden stylus belongs to a king or an emperor.
Gold is too soft and slippery to carve fine letters upon dry palm leaves; my fingers would slip.
My stylus was a plain tool of hardened iron, with a humble handle of neem wood smoothed by thirty years of honest ink.'

Tenali dove a second time, surfacing with an ornate stylus of pure, polished silver with an ivory handle:
'Is this thine?'
Shastriji replied: 'No, master. Silver tarnishes, and its tip is too blunt for my delicate script. That is not mine.'

Tenali dove a third time, bringing up Shastriji’s old, blackened iron stylus with its worn neem handle.
The old scribe let out a cry of pure, joyous relief, clutching the iron tool to his chest as though it were his own child:
'Yes! That is my stylus! That is the breadwinner of my family! With this iron tip, I have copied ten thousand pages of poetry!'

Tenali Raman was moved to tears by the old scribe’s profound, incorruptible honesty and love for his craft.
Tenali presented Shastriji with his old iron stylus, and then handed him the gold and silver styluses as gifts, along with a purse of fifty gold coins from King Krishnadevaraya:
'Shastriji, an honest craftsman who honors the humble tools of his labor is greater than an emperor.
Take the gold to secure thy family’s comfort, and use thine iron stylus to continue copying the wisdom of our ancestors!'

The old scribe blessed Tenali with a full heart, proving that true wealth resides in honest devotion to one’s work.
moral: Honest tools used with devotion are the true wealth of a craftsman; false pride seeks only golden toys.
